newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says Boeing offers not enough, talks continue.
newsitem.headline: EU says Boeing offers not enough, talks continue.

text.p: The European Commission has given Boeing Co a few more hours to make serious concessions over its merger with McDonnell Douglas, failing which it will block the deal, Commission sources said on Tuesday.
Boeing's latest offers to win European Union approval for the $14 billion deal were not good enough to ease the Commission's concerns about its effect on competition, the sources said.

They were speaking after Boeing representatives met the Commission's competition services into the early hours of Tuesday. The Commission plans to take a final decision at its weekly meeting on July 23.

Although the EU has legally until July 31 to give its verdict, the sources argued that it must obtain remedies today at the latest to be able to consult antitrust experts from the 15-nation bloc and respect other strict procedural rules.
"We will see what happens in the next few hours...today is the crucial day," one source said.

The source said in some areas the offers made by Boeing were "not sufficient" and in others "totally insufficient". None of the Commission's three areas of concern had been met, the source said while declining to identify the issues discussed.
"None of those points have been, in a totally satisfactory way, concluded," the source said.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has repeatedly said he would not accept exclusive supply pacts signed between Boeing and U.S. airlines AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines.
Although McDonnell Douglas has become a minor player in the civil aviation sector, the Commission is also concerned that the deal will increase Boeing's customer base to 84 percent from 60 percent.

About 25 percent of all planes in the world's fleets are McDonnells and the Commission fears Boeing will somehow tie the servicing and maintenance of those planes to their replacement by its own aircraft. It also sees McDonnell's spare parts business as a lucrative addition to Boeing's business.
But the Commission sources denied a report in the Financial Times on Tuesday that it proposed a deal under which Boeing would licence a third party to make the parts for McDonnell's planes.
One source said the idea had apparently been expressed to the British newspaper by a legal expert who was not involved in the talks.

The Commission has also warned Boeing it fears spillovers of defence contracts money, of which McDonnell is a key beneficiary, into Boeing's civil aviation business. McDonnell Douglas makes mainly military aircraft.

Some European industry sources believe the problem would be solved only through a clear separation of the new group's military and civil aviation activities. But they thought it was unlikely Boeing would agree to that.

The Commission has been re-discussing with the United States since the beginning of the year a better enforcement of a 1992 bilateral agreement on controlling aircraft subsidies amid European accusations that the U.S. is not respecting the deal.

The Commission insists the resumption of the subsidy talks is totally separate from the merger investigation, which must answer the key question of whether the deal creates or strengthens a dominant position that would harm fair competition in Europe.

Boeing's archrival Airbus has said that the merger is part of a plot, which has the complicity of the U.S. administration, to eliminate it altogether. Airbus is a partnership between Aerospatiale of France, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, British Aerospace and Spain's CASA.

The Commission can prohibit the deal under its merger control law. If Boeing went ahead with the deal regardless of the decision, the Commission could fine it up to 10 percent of turnover and fine also any European companies that did business with it.
